title: Xiaomi Unveils Xring O3 Chip in Latest Push to Build Its Own Smartphone Silicon
excerpt: The third-generation processor, manufactured by TSMC on 3nm, will power an upcoming flagship folding phone as Xiaomi reduces its reliance on Qualcomm and MediaTek.
body:
• Xiaomi unveiled the Xring O3, its third-generation in-house smartphone processor, manufactured by TSMC on a 3-nanometre process.
  • The chip is expected to power Xiaomi's upcoming flagship folding phone, with a shipment target of 200,000 to 300,000 units.
  • Cumulative shipments of devices running the earlier Xring O1 — including phones, tablets, and watches — have surpassed 1 million units since its May 2025 launch.
  • The move deepens Xiaomi's push to reduce reliance on Qualcomm and MediaTek as smartphone makers increasingly develop proprietary silicon.

Xiaomi's Third-Generation Chip Arrives

Xiaomi on Monday unveiled the Xring O3, the latest iteration of its in-house smartphone processor, as the world's third-largest smartphone vendor accelerates efforts to control more of its hardware stack.

https://x.com/UniverseIce/status/2091771619064836596

The chip will be manufactured by Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company using its 3-nanometre production technology, two people familiar with the matter told Reuters. Neither Xiaomi nor TSMC responded to requests for comment on the chip's manufacturer, production technology, or shipment targets.

The Xring O3 is expected to power Xiaomi's upcoming flagship folding phone, with initial shipment targets between 200,000 and 300,000 units, according to the sources.

Building on a Young Track Record

The launch comes roughly a year after Xiaomi introduced the Xring O1, its first proprietary smartphone processor, in May 2025. That chip debuted in the Xiaomi 15S Pro and Xiaomi Pad 7 Ultra, establishing the company as only the fourth smartphone brand globally — after Apple, Qualcomm (through its reference designs), and Huawei — to mass-produce a system-on-chip at the 3nm scale.

Xiaomi said during an earnings call last week that cumulative shipments of devices powered by the Xring O1 had surpassed 1 million units across smartphones, tablets, and watches. Smartphone-specific sales totaled approximately 150,000 units since launch, according to the sources.

At MWC 2026 in March, Xiaomi confirmed plans to release a new version of the chip annually and to deploy its in-house silicon in global markets, not just China — a meaningful expansion given that the 15S Pro was a China-only product.

"This represents yet one more step toward China reaching self-sufficiency in this crucial industry — as well as in broader ICT and electronics supply chains."

— Stephen Ezell, Information Technology and Innovation Foundation

A Broader Industry Shift

Xiaomi's chip push mirrors a wider trend across the smartphone industry. Apple has designed its own processors since 2010. Samsung develops the Exynos line for its Galaxy phones. Huawei resumed domestic chip production with its Kirin series despite U.S. export restrictions. Google's Tensor chips power Pixel devices.

The common thread is reducing dependence on merchant chip suppliers like Qualcomm and MediaTek. For Xiaomi, owning its SoC roadmap provides several strategic advantages: product differentiation in a commoditized Android market, better optimization between hardware and software, and insulation from the geopolitical tensions that continue to reshape semiconductor supply chains.

"Longer term, owning its SoC roadmap will insulate Xiaomi's devices from the U.S.–China geopolitical tensions and help mitigate global supply-chain disruptions," semiconductor analyst Ray Wang told AFP.

TSMC Remains the Linchpin

While Xiaomi designs the Xring chips, TSMC manufactures them — a dependency shared by Apple, AMD, and Nvidia. Chinese domestic foundries like SMIC cannot yet produce chips at the 3nm scale due to U.S. export controls restricting access to advanced lithography equipment.

The Xring O1 used TSMC's N3E process. The O3 stays on the 3nm node rather than moving to 2nm, a decision analysts attribute to cost and production capacity constraints. Apple, Qualcomm, and MediaTek are expected to introduce 2nm chips around September 2026, which could narrow Xiaomi's process advantage in the second half of the year.

What's Next

Xiaomi has invested 13.5 billion yuan (approximately .9 billion) in chip R&D and committed 50 billion yuan over the next decade to build out its semiconductor capabilities. The company is also expanding its AI assistant, Xiao AI, to global markets, with Google's Gemini models reportedly powering the international rollout.

For consumers in India — one of Xiaomi's largest markets — the Xring chip's eventual arrival in global devices could bring tighter hardware-software integration and potentially more competitive pricing as Xiaomi reduces its per-device licensing costs to Qualcomm.
